content.text:
Why is a wind-turbine maker building an AI data centre? <short pause>

In Inner Mongolia, Envision is connecting those businesses through an AI campus called Galaxy.

Follow the electricity to understand why an energy company wants to build it.

<breath> Envision founder and CEO Lei Zhang started the company in 2007, making wind turbines.

It expanded into batteries and energy systems. Computing creates demand for that equipment.

Ulanqab sits about 300 kilometres northwest of Beijing, in China's Inner Mongolia.

SemiAnalysis visited in September 2026. Its report is the starting point for this story.

OpenAI's Stargate is the American comparison. Galaxy is a separate Envision project. <short pause>

SemiAnalysis reports 120 megawatts delivered in August 2026, within a year.

That's power for computing equipment. Megawatts measure the rate of electricity use, not AI performance.

The full plan is 800 megawatts. Used continuously, that matches the annual grid electricity bought by about 650,000 US homes.

Or about 67 stadiums like Munich's Allianz Arena, comparing their maximum available electrical power.

For AI, imagine eight centres using 100 megawatts for computing each. Cooling needs extra power. These are comparisons, not measured usage. <short pause>

<breath> Accelerators process data, with memory and networks keeping them supplied.

Power must reach those racks reliably. Their heat also has to leave the building.

SemiAnalysis describes a five-megawatt pilot testing a different way of supplying the racks.

Solid-state transformers convert incoming alternating current into an 800-volt direct-current bus. <short pause>

At the same power, doubling DC voltage halves the current in a conductor.

At the same resistance, lower current reduces heating losses. Galaxy's actual savings need measuring.

Rack electronics still reduce voltage further before that power reaches the chips.

<breath> Envision also makes turbines and batteries, extending its role beyond owning the building.

The company can coordinate generation, storage and equipment supplying power inside the campus. <short pause>

But a wind farm's rated power is not its output at every moment.

The wind rises and falls. Computing equipment needs reliable power through those changes.

Batteries store some surplus electricity and supply it when generation falls below demand.

Their usefulness depends on power, stored energy, and how long the calm lasts.

'Wind-powered' does not establish that wind supplies all the electricity, every hour. <short pause>

How much of Galaxy is fitted with hardware and actually running remains unverified.

Reported delivered capacity is not a measurement of load drawn by working servers.

Buildings and megawatts cannot confirm installed chips, or how much work they produce.

Envision's larger capacity announcements also need reconciling with SemiAnalysis's description of the campus.

Those are questions for Zhang and the site's engineers, alongside the wider strategy. <short pause>

The next test is how much useful computing this energy system can deliver.

annotations.style: Calm, curious documentary narration. Clear neutral British English. Conversational and connected, with measured emphasis on the explanatory questions. Aim for about 140 words per minute, slowing slightly for electrical units and figures. Keep the same vocal character throughout. Natural light breathing, without theatrical reactions. Pronounce Lei Zhang approximately lay jahng, and Ulanqab approximately oo-lahn-chahb. Read DC as D C, AI as A I, and CEO as C E O. Preserve every qualifier such as reports, planned and unverified.
